Act as a strict, adversarial ACL Main Conference reviewer looking for concrete reasons to REJECT two proposed low-resource NMT training methods for adapting a pretrained multilingual encoder-decoder model to an unseen source language. Neither proposal is established evidence yet.

PROPOSAL 1 — Gold-Ordered Asymmetric Dropout Consistency (GOC):
Given two native dropout forward passes yielding token distributions p_1, p_2 at each supervised target position t with gold token y_t, define the gold-stronger view w_t = argmax_{v in {1,2}} log p_{v,t}(y_t) and weaker view l_t = 3 - w_t (average on ties).
Objective: L_GOC = 0.5*(CE(z_1, y) + CE(z_2, y)) + beta * mean_t KL(sg(p_{w_t, t}) || p_{l_t, t}), where sg is stop-gradient.
Motivation: In symmetric R-Drop SKL(p_1, p_2), the degraded view drags down the gold-aligned view, and the symmetric gradient component (g_1+g_2)/2 suppresses fluctuating rare gold tokens while boosting stable frequent target priors. GOC eliminates both effects while preserving full-vocabulary dark-knowledge transfer. Zero extra parameters, zero inference overhead.

PROPOSAL 2 — Internal Prior-Amplified Margin (IPAM / Self-PoE):
Pass 1 runs native encoder+decoder -> logits z_full. Pass 2 runs decoder-only (torch.no_grad) with all cross-attention residual outputs zeroed -> internal target LM prior logits z_ilm (zero external LM, zero extra parameters, zero inference overhead).
Objective: L_IPAM = (1 - lambda) * CE(z_full, y) + lambda * CE(z_full + alpha * sg(z_ilm), y).
Motivation: On target-predictable function words where z_ilm already predicts y_t, CE(z_full + alpha*z_ilm, y) vanishes while (1-lambda)*CE(z_full, y) preserves inference calibration. On rare source-grounded content words where z_ilm favors a frequent target competitor, adding alpha*sg(z_ilm) amplifies the internal prior competitor and forces encoder cross-attention to build a larger discriminative margin.

Using ONLY the selected primary papers, answer rigorously with section/equation citations where available (mark absent details unknown):
1. For PROPOSAL 1 (GOC): What are the strongest reasons to reject it? Specifically check overlap with R-Drop, unidirectional KL ablations, self-distillation, and whether ordering by gold likelihood creates a hidden confound (e.g., effective CE reweighting, variance collapse, or optimization instability).
2. For PROPOSAL 2 (IPAM): Compare exact formulas and gradient paths against Miao et al. (2021) MTO/MSO, Clark et al. (2019) Product of Experts, Meng et al. (2021) ILME, Baziotis et al. (2020), and Sennrich et al. (2024). What is already established prior, what is genuinely different (if anything), and what are the sharpest failure modes (e.g., out-of-distribution zeroed cross-attention in a pretrained decoder, calibration shift, or memorization)?
3. Do NOT certify novelty. Identify the exact matched controls required to falsify each proposal.

response.answer:
### Meta-Reviewer / Reviewer Evaluation (ACL Main Conference)

**Recommendation:** **STRONG REJECT**  
**Summary of Submissions:** The proposals present two heuristic modifications to sequence-to-sequence training for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation: (1) **Gold-Ordered Asymmetric Dropout Consistency (GOC)**, an asymmetric, stop-gradient variant of R-Drop conditioned on per-token ground-truth likelihood; and (2) **Internal Prior-Amplified Margin (IPAM / Self-PoE)**, a Product-of-Experts loss adding zeroed cross-attention decoder logits to full model logits during training. 

Neither proposal presents established empirical evidence. Both rely on theoretical and causal premises that directly conflict with established findings on consistency regularization, probability calibration, internal language model estimation, and dataset debiasing. 

---

### 1. Detailed Critique of Proposal 1 (GOC)

#### 1.1 Overlap with R-Drop, Unidirectional KL, and Self-Distillation
* **Symmetric Regularization vs. Unidirectional Gradient Halving:** Standard R-Drop minimizes the symmetric bidirectional KL divergence between two stochastic dropout sub-models: \\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = \frac{1}{2}(D_{\text{KL}}(P_1 \parallel P_2) + D_{\text{KL}}(P_2 \parallel P_1))\\) [1, 2]. Liang et al. explicitly establish that R-Drop functions as mutual instance-wise self-distillation [3] and constrained parameter optimization [4, 5], where updating **both** sub-models symmetrically is essential to constrain parameter freedom and bridge the training–inference gap [6, 7]. In Section 2.4 of Liang et al., they specifically critique earlier methods like ELD for only backpropagating through one branch, noting that updating both sub-models provides superior regularization efficiency and stability [7]. GOC discards this foundation by arbitrarily imposing a unidirectional stop-gradient \\(\text{KL}(\text{sg}(p_{w}) \parallel p_l)\\).
* **Degeneracy of Dropout Perturbations as Teacher Targets:** In GOC, \\(p_{w_t}\\) is merely a single stochastic sub-network sampled via native Bernoulli dropout [8]. Unlike true knowledge distillation where the teacher is an ensemble or a converged, larger model [3, 9], a single dropout pass is notoriously high-variance. Freezing \\(p_w\\) with stop-gradient forces the model to treat an instantaneous, noisy dropout configuration as an unshakeable ground-truth teacher over the entire vocabulary.

#### 1.2 The Hidden Confound: Label-Conditioned Selection Bias and Optimization Instability
* **Conditioning Teacher Selection on Gold Tokens (\\(y_t\\)):** GOC dynamically assigns the teacher role via \\(w_t = \operatorname{argmax}_{v \in \{1,2\}} \log p_{v,t}(y_t)\\). The gradient of \\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}, t} = \text{KL}(\text{sg}(p_{w_t, t}) \parallel p_{l_t, t})\\) with respect to the weaker logits \\(z_{l_t}\\) is analytically given by:
\\[\nabla_{z_{l_t}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}, t} = p_{l_t, t} - p_{w_t, t}\\]
Because \\(w_t\\) is selected *specifically* because \\(p_{w_t, t}(y_t) > p_{l_t, t}(y_t)\\), the gradient update along the gold coordinate \\(y_t\\) is strictly:
\\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}, t}}{\partial z_{l_t}(y_t)} = p_{l_t, t}(y_t) - p_{w_t, t}(y_t) < 0\\]
This acts as an **implicit, uncontrolled label-sharpening objective** that operates in direct opposition to label smoothing [10, 11].
* **Variance Collapse and Spurious Confidence in Low-Resource Adaptation:** In low-resource NMT, models overfit rapidly and produce pathology-level overconfident (low-entropy) distributions on small parallel corpora [12, 13]. If a dropout configuration randomly zeroes out contextual gating and spuriously spikes the probability mass on \\(y_t\\) while scrambling the tail, GOC crowns that noisy configuration as the target \\(p_w\\). The weaker view \\(p_l\\) is then forced to mimic the entire distribution of the noisy view. Rather than regularizing the model toward a smoother manifold [14, 15], GOC reinforces stochastic spikes on gold tokens, accelerating overfitting and inducing severe training instability.
* **The "Degraded View Drags Down Gold View" Fallacy:** GOC’s foundational motivation asserts that in symmetric R-Drop, "the degraded view drags down the gold-aligned view." Liang et al. disprove this: the bidirectional KL constraint bounds the empirical loss gap between the full model and sub-models \\(\sqrt{\epsilon}\\) via the Lipschitz constant of the softmax operator [7, 16]. Symmetrizing the gradient updates both parameter states toward a shared flat minimum; it does not suppress rare tokens.

---

### 2. Detailed Critique of Proposal 2 (IPAM / Self-PoE)

#### 2.1 Formal Comparison of Equations and Gradient Paths

| Method | Formulation / Objective | Role & Nature of Prior / Bias | Gradient Path & Execution Stage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **IPAM (Proposal 2)** | \\(\mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\text{CE}(z_{\text{full}}, y) + \lambda\text{CE}(z_{\text{full}} + \alpha \cdot \text{sg}(z_{\text{ilm}}), y)\\) | \\(z_{\text{ilm}}\\) obtained by zeroing cross-attention residuals in the decoder. | Training time. Gradient backpropagates **only** into \\(z_{\text{full}}\\). No external model. |
| **Clark et al. (2019)** [17, 18] | \\(\hat{p} = \text{softmax}(\log p + \log b)\\) (Eq. 3.2.3: Bias Product / Product of Experts). Gradients backpropagate only into robust model \\(p\\); bias model \\(b\\) is frozen [19]. |

Also analyses POSTNORM: \\(p \propto p_{\text{TM}} \cdot p_{\text{LM}}\\) [27]. | External autoregressive LM trained on target monolingual data as a prior. | Training time. Posterior regularization via soft KL constraint; TM free to deviate from prior [28, 29]. |
| **Meng et al. (2021) ILME** [30-32] | \\(\text{Score} = \log P_{\text{E2E}} + \lambda_T \log P_{\text{extLM}} - \lambda_I \log P_{\text{ILM}}\\) (Eq. 18, 33). | Internal LM estimated by eliminating acoustic/context representations (\\(c_u=0\\)). | **Inference time only**. No training loss modification. Standard E2E model unchanged [33, 34]. |
| **Sennrich et al. (2024)** [35] | \\(\text{Score} = \log P(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) - \alpha \log P(y_t \mid x_{\text{rand}}, y_{<t})\\) (Source-Contrastive). | Random/unrelated source segment or incorrect language token. | **Inference time only**. Decoding objective modification; zero retraining or architectural surgery [35]. |

#### 2.2 Prior Art vs. Genuinely Different Aspects
* **What is Already Established Prior:**
  1. The objective structure \\(\text{CE}(z + \alpha \cdot \text{sg}(z_{\text{bias}}), y)\\) is the exact **Bias Product (Product of Experts)** objective introduced by Clark et al. (2019) to factor out superficial dataset biases [18, 36].
  2. The concept of approximating an internal language model by zeroing out encoder context/cross-attention was derived and formalized by Meng et al. (2021) as the Joint Softmax Approximation (JSA) for Attention-based Encoder-Decoder (AED) models [31, 37].
  3. Training an encoder-decoder with a sum of decoder and LM logits was analyzed in NMT by Stahlberg et al. (2018) and Baziotis et al. (2020) under the POSTNORM objective [25, 27].
* **What is "Genuinely Different":**
  - IPAM simply grafts Meng et al.'s inference-time zeroing heuristic directly into Clark et al.'s training-time Product of Experts formula inside a single sequence-to-sequence model.

#### 2.3 Sharpest Failure Modes and Inherent Flaws
1. **Severe Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Degradation in the Decoder:**
   In an Attention-Based Encoder-Decoder (AED) Transformer, decoder layers are trained with residual connections and Layer Normalization conditioned on cross-attention outputs [38]. Meng et al. (2021) explicitly evaluated the internal LM perplexity (ILM-PPL) when zeroing context representations in AED models (Section 5.5, Figure 1b): **AED ILM-PPL exploded to 796.7**, compared to 99.4 for RNN-T and 30.1 for a trained source LM [39, 40]. They proved that an AED decoder *does not function as a standalone LM* without encoder representations [39]. Artificially zeroing cross-attention outputs produces wildly uncalibrated, chaotic logits \\(z_{\text{ilm}}\\). Injecting these uncalibrated logits into the training loss poisons the gradient.
2. **Probability Sharpening, Entropic Collapse, and Inability to Deviate:**
   Baziotis et al. (2020) conducted an extensive analysis of Product-of-Experts / POSTNORM training (\\(\log p \propto \log p_{\text{TM}} + \log p_{\text{LM}}\\)) in low-resource NMT (Section 5, Figure 3, Figure 4) [13, 41, 42]. They proved that adding prior logits during training acts like a logical AND, forcing the model into an ultra-low-entropy state that destroys translation quality [28, 43]. On WMT En–De and En–Tr, POSTNORM caused catastrophic degradation (e.g., dropping En–De BLEU from 26.9 to 24.5) [44]. When target words disagree with the prior (such as rare content words or source-grounded named entities), PoE training assigns high probability to incorrect tokens and severely penalizes legitimate source conditioning [41, 42].
3. **Severe Inference Calibration Shift:**
   In IPAM, the model is trained against the combined logits \\(z_{\text{full}} + \alpha z_{\text{ilm}}\\). The gradient forces \\(z_{\text{full}}\\) to learn the *residual*:
   \\[\nabla_{z_{\text{full}}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{IPAM}} = (1-\lambda)(p_{\text{full}} - y) + \lambda(\text{softmax}(z_{\text{full}} + \alpha z_{\text{ilm}}) - y)\\]
   At inference time, the proposal discards \\(z_{\text{ilm}}\\) and decodes with \\(z_{\text{full}}\\) alone. Because \\(z_{\text{full}}\\) was trained to predict \\(y\\) in the presence of \\(+\alpha z_{\text{ilm}}\\), removing \\(\alpha z_{\text{ilm}}\\) at test time creates a severe test-time logit shift, destroying model calibration and beam search performance.
4. **Failure Modes of Bias Product / Over-Compensation:**
   Clark et al. (2019, Section 5.1) demonstrated that when the bias is not strictly conditionally independent of the main features (the "Dependent Bias" setting), the Bias Product method causes the robust model to become *anti-correlated* with the bias, over-compensating and actively learning to undo the bias model's errors [45]. Because cross-attention is fragile in low-resource adaptation to an unseen source language, adding a degraded internal prior will cause cross-attention either to over-compensate erratically or overfit to training artifacts.

---

### 3. Matched Experimental Controls Required to Falsify the Proposals

Novelty cannot be certified for either proposal. To prevent rejection, an empirical submission must evaluate against the following rigorous, matched baselines:

#### For Proposal 1 (GOC):
1. **Symmetric R-Drop (Liang et al., 2021) [46]:** Compute-matched and hyperparameter-tuned (\\(\alpha \in \{1, 3, 5\}\\)) standard bidirectional R-Drop [2, 47].
2. **Unidirectional R-Drop with Random Orientation:** Optimize \\(\text{KL}(\text{sg}(p_1) \parallel p_2)\\) with random view orientation rather than gold likelihood ordering. This isolates whether stopping gradients itself has any effect independent of gold selection.
3. **Reverse-GOC Control:** Set \\(w_t = \operatorname{argmin}_{v \in \{1,2\}} \log p_{v,t}(y_t)\\) (transferring from the gold-weaker to the gold-stronger view). If the author's hypothesis—that weaker views drag down stronger views—is correct, Reverse-GOC must catastrophically underperform GOC. If Reverse-GOC performs comparably, the claimed mechanism is falsified and any effect is an artifact of gradient filtering.
4. **Confidence-Penalized Label Smoothing (Szegedy et al., 2016; Baziotis et al., 2020) [10, 11]:** Since GOC implicitly sharpens updates on \\(y_t\\), it must be compared against tuned label smoothing (\\(\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.1, 0.2\}\\)) to prove the gain is not trivial label-distribution re-scaling.
5. **Double-Batch Standard Training (Liang et al., 2021, Appendix C.1) [16]:** A baseline doubling the mini-batch size without KL loss to isolate whether gains stem simply from processing \\(2\times\\) the forward instances per step.

#### For Proposal 2 (IPAM):
1. **Auxiliary LM Baseline (Miao et al., 2021 MTO/MSO) [23]:** A jointly trained auxiliary decoder sharing embeddings and output projections without cross-attention. This isolates whether zeroing cross-attention in an integrated decoder introduces harmful out-of-distribution representations compared to a properly trained architectural prior.
2. **Inference-Time Internal LM Estimation (Meng et al., 2021 ILME) [30]:** Standard fine-tuning without IPAM, subtracting \\(\lambda_I z_{\text{ilm}}\\) only during inference beam search (Eq. 33) [32]. This verifies whether intrusive training-time PoE is even necessary or inferior to inference-time subtraction.
3. **Posterior Regularization via Soft KL (Baziotis et al., 2020) [26]:** Replacing the PoE term with a KL penalty against an external target LM (\\(D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\text{TM}} \parallel p_{\text{LM}})\\)) to verify whether preserving model flexibility and inference calibration outperforms hard logit addition.
4. **Static / Unigram Prior Control:** Replacing \\(z_{\text{ilm}}\\) with static target marginal log-frequencies. This determines whether IPAM is merely acting as a crude frequency-based competitor penalty rather than a meaningful contextual LM prior.
5. **Target-Side Word Dropout & Minimum Risk Training (MRT) (Wang & Sennrich, 2020; Voita et al., 2021) [48, 49]:** Established training methods proven to prevent over-reliance on target history and reduce hallucinations without perturbing cross-attention manifolds [48, 50].

---
Would you like me to formalize these failure modes into a complete reviewer report draft with targeted revision experiments?

our R-Drop to regularize the output predictions of sub models from dropout.

Unlike previous researches of designing specific dropout variants or adapting dropout to different
applications, we consider to further regularize the model on the success of dropout. Specifically, any
two sub models sampled from dropout are encouraged to produce consistent model prediction for an
input data by utilizing KL-divergence in the training stage. That is, we conduct regularization on the
model output level. In doing so, the sub model outputs produced by the randomness of dropout are
regularized to reduce the parameter freedom, which will enhance generalization in inference.

with the assistance of the LM, the motivation is that

This formulation gives flexibility to the model,
unlike probability interpolation, such as in fusion
methods. For example, POSTNORM multiplies the
probabilities of the LM and TM, which is the same
as applying a logical AND operation, where only
words that are probable under both distributions
will receive non-negligible probabilities. This pre-
vents the model from generating the correct word
when there is a large “disagreement” between the
TM and the LM, which is inevitable as the LM is not
aware of the source sentence (i.e., unconditional).
However, by using the LM-prior we do not change
the outputs of the TM. LKL pushes the TM to stay on average close to the prior, but crucially, it en-
ables the TM to deviate from it when needed, for
example to copy words from the source.

7 Conclusions In this work, we present a simple approach for in-
corporating knowledge from monolingual data to
NMT. Specifically, we use a LM trained on target-
side monolingual data, to regularize the output dis-
tributions of a TM. This method is more efficient
than alternative approaches that used pretrained
LMs, because it is not required during inference.
Also, we avoid the translation errors introduced by
LM-fusion, because the TM is able to deviate from
the prior when needed. We empirically show that while this method
works by simply changing the training objective, it
achieves better results than alternative LM-fusion
techniques. Also, it yields consistent performance
gains even with modest monolingual data (3M sen-
tences) across all translation directions. This makes
it useful for low-resource languages, where not
only parallel but also monolingual data are scarce.

Inspired by HAT, we propose an internal LM estimation (ILME) method to effectively integrate external LMs with all pre-existing
E2E models without any additional model training, including the
most popular time-synchoronrous RNN-T and time-asynchonrous
AED. With ILME, we estimate and subtract the internal LM scores
of an E2E model from the log-linear combination of the E2E and
LM scores during inference. By removing the separable AM-LM assumption, ILME enables a more accurate and a lighter-weight ex-
ternal LM integration than Density Ratio with no additional source-
domain LM running at the inference. We evaluate 30K-hour RNN-T
and AED models on cross-domain LibriSpeech test sets and intra-
domain Microsoft production test sets. ILME achieves up to 15.5%
and 6.8% relative word error rate (WER) reductions from Shallow
Fusion for cross- and intra-domain evaluations, respectively. Fur-
ther, despite having 26.8%-29.8% fewer parameters, ILME consis-
tently outperforms Density Ratio in terms of lower WER.

6. CONCLUSION We propose an internal LM estimation method to effectively inte-
grate an external LM with all pre-existing E2E models without any
additional training. The internal LM is approximated by the output
of an E2E model when zeroing out its acoustic components. Dur-
ing inference, the internal LM score is subtracted from the log-linear
combination of E2E model and LM scores. We evaluate 30K-hour
RNN-T and AED models on cross-domain LibriSpeech test sets and
intra-domain Microsoft production test sets with different LM in-
tegration methods. ILME reduces the WER of Shallow Fusion by
8.1%-15.5% relatively in cross-domain evaluations, and 2.4%-6.8%
relatively in intra-domain evaluations. Further, ILME consistently
outperforms Density Ratio in terms of better WER despite having
26.8%-29.8% fewer run-time parameters.

View a PDF of the paper titled Mitigating Hallucinations and Off-target Machine Translation with Source-Contrastive and Language-Contrastive Decoding, by Rico Sennrich and Jannis Vamvas and Alireza Mohammadshahi View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Hallucinations and off-target translation remain unsolved problems in MT, especially for low-resource languages and massively multilingual models. In this paper, we introduce two related methods to mitigate these failure cases with a modified decoding objective, without either requiring retraining or external models. In source-contrastive decoding, we search for a translation that is probable given the correct input, but improbable given a random input segment. In language-contrastive decoding, we search for a translation that is probable, but improbable given the wrong language indicator token. Experiments on the massively multilingual models M2M-100 (418M) and SMaLL-100 show that these methods suppress hallucinations and off-target translations, reducing the number of translations with segment-level chrF2 below 10 by 67-83% on average, and the number of translations with oscillatory hallucinations by 75-92% on average, across 57 tested translation directions. In a proof of concept on out-of-English translation, we also show that we can suppress off-target translations with large language models. We release our source code at this https URL .

R-Drop: Regularized Dropout for Neural Networks Xiaobo Liang 1∗ Lijun Wu 2∗ Juntao Li 1 Yue Wang 1 Qi Meng 2 Tao Qin 2 Wei Chen 2 Min Zhang 1 Tie-Yan Liu 2 1Soochow University, 2Microsoft Research Asia Abstract Dropout is a powerful and widely used technique to regularize the training of deep
neural networks. Though effective and performing well, the randomness introduced
by dropout causes unnegligible inconsistency between training and inference. In
this paper, we introduce a simple consistency training strategy to regularize dropout,
namely R-Drop, which forces the output distributions of different sub models gen-
erated by dropout to be consistent with each other. Specifically, for each training
sample, R-Drop minimizes the bidirectional KL-divergence between the output dis-
tributions of two sub models sampled by dropout. Theoretical analysis reveals that
R-Drop reduces the above inconsistency. Experiments on 5 widely used deep learn-
ing tasks ( 18 datasets in total), including neural machine translation, abstractive
summarization, language understanding, language modeling, and image classifica-
tion, show that R-Drop is universally effective. In particular, it yields substantial
improvements when applied to fine-tune large-scale pre-trained models, e.g., ViT,
RoBERTa-large, and BART, and achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performances
with the vanilla Transformer model on WMT14 English→German translation
( 30.91 BLEU) and WMT14 English→French translation ( 43.95 BLEU), even
surpassing models trained with extra large-scale data and expert-designed advanced
variants of Transformer models. Our code is available at GitHub 2.

4.5 Effect of Weight α Further, we investigate the impact of the KL-divergence loss weight α. As mentioned in Section 3.1, we set α = 5 for NMT experiments.
Here we vary the α in {1, 3, 5, 7, 10} and conduct experiments. As
shown in Table 7, small α ( e.g., 1) can not perform as good as large α ( e.g., 5), which means we should pay more attention to the KL-
divergence regularization. However, too much regularization ( α = 10)
is also not good, and the best balanced choice is α = 5. Note that
the choice of α is distinct for different tasks (e.g., NMT, language
understanding), which depends on how easy the over-fitting happens
caused by the specific data size and model size of each task.

5 Exposure Bias and Source Contributions The results in the previous section agree with some
observations made in previous work studying self-
recovery and hallucinations. In this section, we
illustrate more explicitly how our methodology can
be used to shed light on the effects of exposure bias
and training objectives. Wang and Sennrich (2020) empirically link the
hallucination mode to exposure bias (Ranzato et al.,
2016), i.e. the mismatch between the gold history
seen at training time, and the (potentially erro-
neous) model-generated prefixes at test time. The
authors hypothesize that exposure bias leads to
an over-reliance on target history, and show that
Minimum Risk Training (MRT), which does not
suffer from exposure bias, reduces hallucinations.
However, they did not directly measure this over-
reliance on target history. Our method is able to di-
rectly test whether there is indeed an over-reliance
on the target history with MLE-trained models, and
more robust inclusion of source context with MRT.
We also consider a simpler heuristic, word dropout,
which we hypothesize to have a similar effect.

Random prefixes. We see that, among all mod-
els, the MRT model has the highest influence of
source (Figure 5a) and the most focused source
contributions (Figure 5b). This agrees with our
expectations: by construction, MRT removes ex-
posure bias completely. Therefore, it is confused
by random prefixes less than other models. Ad-
ditionally, this also links to Wang and Sennrich
(2020) who showed that MRT reduces hallucina-
tions. When using word dropout, both its variants
also increase the influence of source, but to a much
lesser extent (Figure 5a). As expected, since target-
side word dropout slightly reduces exposure bias
(in contrast to source-side word dropout), it leads
to a larger increase of source influence.
